questions.question_text: What is 13 % 4?
questions.explanation: 13 ÷ 4 = 3 remainder 1, so 13 % 4 = 1. Modulus returns the remainder after division.

questions.question_text: Which expression evaluates to 2.5?
questions.explanation: (double) 5 / 2 casts 5 to a double before dividing → 2.5. 5/2 is integer division (2); 5%2 is 1; 5/2.0 = 2.5 but minus 0.5 = 2.0.

questions.question_text: What is the value of (int) 4.99 + (int) 0.99?
questions.explanation: (int) truncates: 4.99 → 4 and 0.99 → 0, so 4 + 0 = 4. Casting to int drops the decimal (no rounding) before addition.

questions.question_text: What does "COMPUTER".substring(2, 5) return?
questions.explanation: Indices 2,3,4 (end exclusive): C(0)O(1)M(2)P(3)U(4) → 'M','P','U' = "MPU". The character at index 5 (T) is excluded.

questions.question_text: Math.max(3, 7) returns:
questions.explanation: Math.max returns the larger of two values: max(3, 7) = 7. Math.min would return the smaller (3).

questions.question_text: Integer.parseInt("25") returns a value of type:
questions.explanation: parseInt converts a String to an int (25). This enables arithmetic; without parsing, "25" would only support String operations like concatenation.

questions.question_text: What prints? int x = 8; if (x > 10) System.out.print("big"); else if (x > 5) System.out.print("medium"); else System.out.print("small");
questions.explanation: x=8: first condition (x>10) false, second (x>5) true → prints 'medium'. The ladder runs the first true branch and skips the rest.

questions.question_text: true && false evaluates to:
questions.explanation: && (AND) is true only if BOTH operands are true; since one is false, the result is false.

questions.question_text: What is the final value? int total = 0; for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++) total += i * i;
questions.explanation: Sums squares: 1+4+9+16+25 = 55. Each iteration adds i² for i from 1 to 5.

questions.question_text: How many times does the inner statement run? for(int i=0;i<4;i++) for(int j=0;j<i;j++) count++;
questions.explanation: Inner loop runs 0,1,2,3 times for i=0,1,2,3 → 0+1+2+3 = 6. Starting j at 0 and bounding by i gives a triangular count.

questions.question_text: Which statement immediately exits a loop entirely?
questions.explanation: break exits the loop entirely; continue skips to the next iteration. They control loop flow differently.

questions.question_text: A no-argument constructor is one that:
questions.option_b: takes no parameters and often sets default field values
questions.explanation: A no-arg constructor takes no parameters; Java provides one by default only if you write no constructors. It typically initializes fields to defaults.

questions.question_text: If a class has fields x and y, 'this.x = x' inside a constructor:
questions.option_b: assigns the parameter x to the instance field x (disambiguating same names)
questions.explanation: 'this.x' refers to the instance field, distinguishing it from the parameter x of the same name. This pattern is common in constructors and setters.

questions.question_text: What is printed? int[] a = {7, 3, 9}; int sum = 0; for (int v : a) sum += v; System.out.println(sum);
questions.explanation: The for-each adds each element: 7+3+9 = 19. It iterates over values directly without indices.

questions.question_text: What does this do? int[] a={4,8,2,6}; for(int i=0;i<a.length-1;i++) if(a[i]>a[i+1]){int t=a[i];a[i]=a[i+1];a[i+1]=t;}
questions.option_b: performs one pass of a bubble sort, swapping adjacent out-of-order pairs
questions.explanation: Comparing and swapping adjacent elements is one pass of bubble sort. After one pass {4,8,2,6} becomes {4,2,6,8} (the largest bubbles toward the end).

questions.question_text: int[] nums = new int[4]; What is nums[2] immediately after this declaration?
questions.explanation: Java initializes int array elements to 0 by default. So nums[2] is 0 before any assignment.

questions.question_text: After list = [3, 6, 9], what does list.add(5) do?
questions.explanation: The single-argument add appends to the end. add(index, value) would insert at a position; here 5 goes to the end.

questions.question_text: Why use an ArrayList instead of an array when the number of elements is unknown?
questions.option_b: ArrayLists resize dynamically as elements are added or removed
questions.explanation: ArrayLists grow and shrink automatically, ideal when the size isn't known in advance. Arrays have a fixed length set at creation.

questions.question_text: For int[][] g = {{1,2,3},{4,5,6}}, what is g.length * g[0].length?
questions.explanation: g.length = 2 rows, g[0].length = 3 columns; 2 × 3 = 6 total elements. Multiplying dimensions gives the element count.

questions.question_text: To access the bottom-right element of int[][] m with R rows and C columns, use:
questions.explanation: The last valid indices are length-1 for each dimension: m[m.length-1][m[0].length-1]. Using R and C directly goes out of bounds (off-by-one).

questions.question_text: If class Cat extends Animal and overrides makeSound(), then Animal a = new Cat(); a.makeSound() runs:
questions.option_b: Cat's makeSound (dynamic dispatch on the actual object)
questions.explanation: Polymorphism dispatches to the actual object's (Cat's) overridden method at runtime, regardless of the Animal reference type.

questions.question_text: A subclass can access a superclass's private fields:
questions.explanation: Private fields aren't directly accessible even to subclasses; they must use inherited public or protected accessor methods. This preserves encapsulation.

questions.question_text: int f(int n){ if(n<=0) return 0; return 2 + f(n-1);} What is f(4)?
questions.explanation: Adds 2 four times: 2+2+2+2+0 = 8. The base case f(0)=0 stops it; each call adds 2 as the stack unwinds.

questions.question_text: What does this print for printNum(3)? void printNum(int n){ if(n>0){ printNum(n-1); System.out.print(n);}}
questions.explanation: The print is AFTER the recursive call, so output happens on the way back up: 123. The deepest call (n=1) prints first.

questions.question_text: What is the result of "Score: " + 5 + 3?
questions.explanation: Left to right: "Score: " + 5 = "Score: 5" (concatenation once a String appears), then + 3 = "Score: 53". Both numbers are concatenated, not added.

questions.question_text: What is !(x < 0) equivalent to?
questions.explanation: Negating < gives >=: !(x < 0) is x >= 0. Negation reverses the operator and flips boundary inclusion.

questions.question_text: An object is created from a class using the keyword:
questions.explanation: The 'new' keyword instantiates an object by invoking a constructor (e.g., new Dog()). It allocates memory and returns a reference.

questions.question_text: Which finds the largest value in int[] a correctly?
questions.option_b: start max at a[0], then compare each element
questions.explanation: Initializing max to a[0] handles arrays with all-negative values; starting at 0 would wrongly return 0 for an all-negative array. Then compare each element to update max.

questions.question_text: The relationship 'a Car has-an Engine' is best modeled with:
questions.option_b: composition (the Car contains an Engine object)
questions.explanation: 'Has-a' relationships use composition (one class holds an instance of another). 'Is-a' relationships use inheritance. Choosing correctly is a key design decision.
